cur:manuscripts-egberti-deposition-entom.summary: Above, Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus lower the body of Christ from the cross; below, in a garden labelled 'hortus', the two men lay Christ, wrapped in a shroud, into a green sarcophagus between two trees. The two scenes are stacked in one tall frame.
facts: The Codex Egberti, a Gospel lectionary made for Archbishop Egbert of Trier, is described as the oldest surviving New Testament picture cycle of the life of Christ in the Ottonian era: 52 of its 60 paintings illustrate Gospel readings in the order of the church year.
During the Second World War the codex was evacuated to Giessen University Library, survived its bombing in December 1944, and was brought back to Trier in May 1945 from a parsonage at Elkerhausen.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-32-christ.summary: The Christ-Logos, nimbed and carrying a cross-staff, stands in a mandorla with angels before the drawn curtains of a tabernacle and 'looketh upon all the inhabitants of the earth'. Below, the psalmist with a harp gazes up at him and points to musicians singing a new song, while a personification of the sea, riding a sea monster, pours out water. It is a joyful drawing of praise.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
Its text is written in rustic capitals, an archaic script that once led scholars to date the manuscript to the 6th century; the drawings are now recognised as Carolingian.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-32-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

vam:O109440.summary: This gilt-bronze processional cross, with a spike at its foot for mounting on a staff, carries on its front a figure of the crucified Christ wearing a tunic, a sign of his kingship and triumph over death, his feet resting on a head that may stand for the skull of Golgotha. The arms are engraved on both faces: the Virgin Mary and St John on the front, and on the back the Lamb of God in a central roundel with the symbols of the four Evangelists. Carried in procession, it brought the image of the Saviour before the faithful.
facts: The V&A notes that, as was common in the early Middle Ages, Christ is shown clothed rather than in a loincloth, expressing his kingship and victory over death.
The cross is discussed in Peter Bloch's corpus of Romanesque bronze crucifixes (Romanische Bronze-Kruzifixe, 1992, no. II D 1).
vam:O109440.notes: The worklist thumbnail (2006AA8669) shows the BACK of the cross, on which Christ does not appear (Lamb of God and Evangelist symbols). The V&A front view (2006AA7697: https://framemark.vam.ac.uk/collections/2006AA7697/full/!600,600/0/default.jpg) shows the crucified Christ and should be used instead. V&A: South Italy, 10th or 11th century.

feat:sarcophagus-of-junius-bassus.summary: Carved for a high Roman official who was baptized shortly before his death, this marble coffin arranges ten biblical scenes in two tiers of columned niches. At the center Christ appears as a youthful, beardless sovereign enthroned above the personified sky, giving the law to Peter and Paul, and below he rides into Jerusalem in humble triumph. It is perhaps the most celebrated early Christian sarcophagus and a masterpiece of the classical style turned to the service of the Gospel.
facts: Its inscription records that Junius Bassus, Prefect of the City of Rome, died in 359 at the age of 42, 'newly baptized' (neofitus).
The Passion is told without a crucifixion: Christ is shown calmly before Pontius Pilate, emphasizing his dignity rather than his suffering.
Beneath the enthroned Christ's feet a bearded figure holds a billowing cloak over his head: Caelus, the Roman personification of the heavens, signaling that Christ rules over the cosmos.
The sarcophagus, originally placed in or beneath Old St. Peter's Basilica, was rediscovered in 1597.
